title: Cook Ding's knife
hook: a cook's blade stays sharp for nineteen years because he cuts through the gaps, never the bone (Zhuangzi 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was wùhuà, the transformation of things: Zhuangzi woke unsure who had dreamed whom. Your line was who is dreaming.

A chef dices an onion without looking. A mechanic hears what's wrong before opening the hood. A dancer lands without a sound. Somewhere along the way, skill stops looking like effort and starts looking like music. In the book of Zhuangzi, a lord named Wenhui watches his cook carving an ox. It's a butcher's story, fair warning, and not everyone loves that. But watch the cook. Every touch of his hand, every shift of his shoulder, every step, every thrust of the knife, falls into rhythm, like a dance. The lord is amazed.
screen: `SKILL THAT LOOKS LIKE MUSIC.` → `LORD WENHUI WATCHES.` → `THE COOK MOVES LIKE A DANCE.`

segments.voice: Wonderful, says the lord. So this is how far skill can go! Cook Ding puts down his knife and says, more or less: what I care about is the Way, and that goes beyond skill. When I started, all I could see was the whole ox. After three years, I no longer saw the whole ox. Now I don't look with my eyes at all. I follow the natural lines. I slide the blade into the big hollows and guide it through the openings, going along with how the thing is made. I never touch a tendon, let alone hit a bone. Then comes the knife. A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes it every month, because he hacks. I've had this knife for nineteen years. I've carved thousands of oxen. And the blade is as sharp as if it just came off the grindstone. Why? There are spaces between the joints, and the edge of the blade has almost no thickness. Put something with no thickness into a space, and there's more than enough room. And at a hard spot, a tangle, he doesn't force it. He slows down. He looks carefully. He moves the knife very slightly, and it comes apart. The lord says: now I've learned how to care for a life. That's the point. Not butchery. How to move through a day. You can hack at every problem, and wear yourself out every month. Or you can look for the gaps: the openings in how things already are.
screen: `THE WAY GOES BEYOND SKILL.` · `NOT THE WHOLE OX.` · `NINETEEN YEARS, STILL SHARP.` · `AT THE HARD SPOT, SLOW DOWN.` · then, large: `FIND THE GAPS.`

segments.voice: Pick something you've been hacking at, an email, a messy room, a hard conversation, and picture it the way Cook Ding sees an ox: not one big lump, but parts with spaces between them. Where's the natural opening, the first easy piece, the tangle where you'll need to slow down? Don't do it yet; just find the grain.
Cook Ding. A butcher whose knife stayed sharp for nineteen years, because it slid through the gaps instead of hacking at the bone.
Your line: find the gaps. The knife lasts because it never fights the bone. Day fifty-one, in the books.

howItsDone: Cook Ding's story comes from chapter three of the Zhuangzi, and in Chinese the phrase "Cook Ding carves the ox" is still used for work done with effortless mastery; Taoist teachers read it as a picture of moving with the grain of things.
